soil-agri-181.title: Legume cover crops, from cowpeas to clovers
soil-agri-181.text: A cover crop that feeds the next crop is hard to beat, which is why legumes, the nitrogen-fixing family in {{ref:soil-bio-182}}, are so often chosen. They sort into three groups. Summer annuals include soybeans, cowpeas and sunn hemp. Winter annuals include winter field peas, crimson clover and hairy vetch. Perennials include red clover, white clover and alfalfa. Sweet yellow clover is a biennial. Austrian winter and Canadian field peas can leave 2.5 tons or more of dry matter and fix 100-150 or more pounds of nitrogen per acre. Each species has limits. Crimson clover matures quickly but is marginal in hardiness zone 5 and on poorly drained or calcareous soils. Cowpeas thrive in heat and drought, yet even mild frost kills them. Sweet clover needs near-neutral pH and does poorly in wet clayey soils, though its roots penetrate compacted subsoil. Red clover starts slowly, so it is interseeded into small grains in early spring.

soil-agri-199.title: Old rotations and the corn-soybean rotation
soil-agri-199.text: A five- to seven-year rotation once kept northern Midwest and Northeast mixed farms in balance. Nitrogen-hungry corn followed pasture, grain grew only two years in five to seven, and oats served as a nurse crop when hay was seeded. It roughly maintained organic matter. Cheap pesticides and fertilizer, feedlots, export markets and price-support programs then narrowed production to corn and soybeans. That pair beats monoculture, but it brings erosion, nitrate and herbicide pollution, organic matter loss and sometimes more insects. Soybeans leave minimal residue. Each farm's soil, climate and economics differ, so these are examples to learn from, not recipes.

soil-agri-192.title: Crop diversification in time and space
soil-agri-192.text: Diversity can be added to a farm in time, in space, or both. Cover crops and rotations diversify over time; different crops in different fields or strips diversify across the landscape. A staggered rotation gives both. Perennials add diversity with less frequent rotations, as when dairy farmers grow alfalfa three to four years before corn. Agroforestry and integrated livestock add further dimensions. Behind all of this sits an ecological principle: diversity contributes to stability and productivity.

soil-agri-198.title: Designing a crop rotation: the main rules
soil-agri-198.text:
A new rotation starts from a few guidelines. Follow a legume forage with a high-nitrogen crop such as corn, and grow oats, barley and wheat less in the second or third year after the sod. Grow the same annual crop only one year, and avoid closely related species in sequence, since they share pests and diseases. Western corn rootworm populations have lately emerged that survive corn-soybean alternation. Before carrots or lettuce, plant grains that root-knot nematodes cannot feed on for a few years.

Use each crop for what it does. Small grains suppress weeds, row crops allow cultivation, and mowed or grazed sods control annual weeds. Use longer perennial periods on sloping, erosive land. Deep-rooted crops such as alfalfa, safflower or sunflower scavenge subsoil nutrients and water, and their root channels aid infiltration.

Where rain is limited, water use is critical. Hay and sunflowers may leave too little moisture, and under 25% of rain during the 14-month fallow in the Central High Plains reaches the next wheat crop.

soil-agri-194.title: Active rooting period: how long roots live in a rotation
soil-agri-194.text: Some rotations keep living roots in the soil for under a third of the time. The active rooting period is the percent of a rotation during which living roots are present. It runs from 32% for corn-soybeans to 57% for soybean-wheat and 76% for a three-year soybean-wheat-corn rotation. Adding winter wheat to a corn-soybean alternation greatly lengthens it, because winter annuals, perennials and cover crops extend the growing period beyond summer annuals. Dry beans-winter wheat with a cover crop reached 92% with three species. Longer living cover decreases erosion, nitrate loss and groundwater contamination.

soil-agri-196.title: What diversified rotations cost and save in labor
soil-agri-196.text: A varied rotation makes the farm calendar easier to live with. Forage hay and early-harvested crops spread labor over the season, which eases management by family labor and gives steadier income. The costs are real, though: more equipment, and labor conflicts such as cultivating corn at the same time as harvesting hay. Integrated livestock with multi-species grazing need less specialized equipment, harvest and spread manure themselves, and diversify income.

soil-agri-195.title: How rotations protect water and cut nitrous oxide
soil-agri-195.text: In South Dakota, a four-year rotation of corn, field pea, winter wheat and soybean beat corn-soybean. It gave higher soybean yield, more soil organic matter and less nitrous oxide lost. Water quality is a big part of the reason. Spring-planted annuals leave soil without roots for much of the year, so nitrate can leach ({{ref:soil-agri-022}}), a problem accentuated by tile drainage in the Midwest and Northeast. Bare wetter soil also runs off and erodes more. Perennial forages and winter grains protect water. Cover crops help similarly but do not substitute for a good rotation, and the combination gives the greatest improvement.

soil-agri-190.title: When cover crops cause trouble
soil-agri-190.text: A cover crop is not free. It can deplete soil moisture, become a weed, compete with an intercropped cash crop for water, light and nutrients, and cost money for seed and establishment. In dry areas and on sands, late killing of a winter cover may cause moisture deficiency. In warm humid no-till climates, longer growth means less wet soil at planting and more residue. The benefits are real too: cover crops raise infiltration through macropores and water-holding capacity through organic matter, and residue slows runoff. Careful management decides which side wins.

soil-agri-185.title: Cover crop mixtures: pairing a grass with a legume
soil-agri-185.text: Mixing species gives a cover crop more than one job, and the most common pairing is a grass with a legume. Mixed stands usually suppress weeds better than a single species, and legumes with small grains offset the nitrogen decline when grains mature. In the mid-Atlantic, a rye-hairy vetch mix manages nitrogen on its own. Rye is stimulated when much nitrate remains, reducing leaching, while vetch competes better and fixes more when little is available. Erect rye also supports vetch, and vetch held up by rye is killed more easily by close mowing, which may replace herbicide in no-till.

soil-agri-187.title: When to plant a cover crop
soil-agri-187.text: A cover crop can fill a whole growing season, follow the cash crop harvest, or be interseeded into a growing cash crop. A full-season high-biomass mix builds the most organic matter and suits infertile or eroded soils and organic transition, but no income crop grows that year. Most farmers instead sow after harvest, avoiding competition with the main crop. Seed can be no-till drilled for better stands, and tillage before seeding should be avoided. The right choice depends on the goal, the cash crops, the season length and the climate.

soil-agri-189.title: Ending a cover crop: termination methods
soil-agri-189.text: Every cover crop has to stop before the cash crop can thrive. Termination kills or drastically weakens it before or during soil preparation. Methods include mowing after flowering, herbicide with no-till, plowing in, mow-roll-crimp with no-till planting in one pass, and winter injury. Waiting a week or two lets residue decompose, which eases nitrogen immobilization, allelopathy, damping-off, cutworm and wireworm problems, and gives a better seedbed. A sudex cover crop is especially allelopathic, so tomatoes, broccoli and lettuce should wait six to eight weeks.

soil-agri-191.title: Choosing cover crops to limit nematodes
soil-agri-191.text: Whether a cover crop helps or harms depends on how well nematodes can feed on it. Grain crops are nonhosts of the root-knot nematode (M. hapla), so growing grains reduces numbers, though very bad infestations may need two full grain seasons. The root-lesion nematode (P. penetrans) infects most crops. A legume such as hairy vetch will stimulate it, while sudangrass, sorghum-sudan, ryegrass and pearl millet reportedly cut numbers. Suppression comes from poor host status, stimulated microbial antagonists and toxic products released on decomposition. Brassicas and pearl millet also biofumigate. For the pests themselves, see {{ref:soil-bio-194}}.

soil-agri-188.title: Planting green into a living cover crop
soil-agri-188.text: Planting green means seeding a cash crop directly into a still-living cover crop and terminating the cover soon after. Older advice left a week or two between killing the cover and planting, which remains best in a dry spring. Now the cover is usually sprayed shortly after planting, or suppressed mechanically with a rolling stalk chopper or a cereal-rye roller-crimper ahead of a no-till planter. It has worked for soybeans, corn and cotton but is not recommended for most direct-seeded vegetables.

soil-agri-183.title: Buckwheat, the fast frost-sensitive cover
soil-agri-183.text: Buckwheat finishes quickly. It takes about six weeks from planting in warm soil to early flowering, and it can exceed 2 feet in a month. This frost-sensitive summer annual grows better than many cover crops on low-fertility soils but tolerates compaction poorly. It competes well with weeds and has been reported to suppress root pathogens including Thielaviopsis and Rhizoctonia. Its seeds do not persist for years, yet it can reseed as a volunteer weed, so mow, roll or till it before seeds develop.

soil-agri-184.title: Groundcovers in orchards and vineyards
soil-agri-184.text: Between the rows of an orchard or vineyard, a perennial groundcover can improve soil health and crop quality. The ideal cover does not overly compete with the main crop and persists with little maintenance. It gives erosion and weed control and tolerates shade, traffic and drought. Acting as a living mulch ({{ref:soil-fert-069}}), Dutch white clover gives modest nitrogen, and low-growing fescues with dense fine roots need minimal mowing. In vineyards covers are sometimes kept away from the vines but used to compete with them and curb excess vegetative growth.

soil-agri-197.title: Rotation as a tool against plant disease
soil-agri-197.text: Some diseases need only a one-year break from their host; others need several years of nonhost crops to cut inoculum. That is why careful rotations, especially alternating grains and broadleaf plants, help control plant diseases and nematodes (see {{ref:soil-agri-004}}). Pulse crops seem to stimulate beneficial organisms and reduce cereal root disease, and a multiyear broadleaf break lowers common root rot of wheat and barley. Rotation has limits. It is hard for wide-host-range pathogens, seed-borne disease and windborne wheat leaf rust, which need other tactics.

soil-agri-202.title: Faidherbia albida, the dry-season shade tree
soil-agri-202.text: Faidherbia albida is a tropical legume tree of seasonally dry climates, used in silvopasture and alley cropping. Its feathery leaves give a light canopy for corn or pasture, and it has a deep taproot. It carries foliage in the dry season when forage is scarce, blooms for bees at the dry season's end, and gives pods for livestock and wood for fuel.

soil-agri-201.title: Forest farming under the canopy
soil-agri-201.text: Forest farming grows crops in the understory of an established natural or timber forest, with no separate growing zones. Here shade is wanted, not avoided. Examples are ginseng, mushrooms, elderberries, rhododendrons and moss, many quite profitable.

soil-agri-200.title: Silvopasture: trees and grazing together
soil-agri-200.text: Silvopasture integrates trees and grazing livestock on the same land. It gives forest products and forage, so both short- and long-term income. Partial shade helps cool-season grasses in heat in temperate climates, and keeps animals cool in hot ones. It still needs agronomic care such as forage selection, fertilization and rotational grazing, and it can stabilize landslide-prone slopes.

soil-agri-203.title: Agroforestry systems that change as trees grow
soil-agri-203.text: Trees change the field as they grow, and transitional systems make use of that shading and microclimate change. A landowner may start with alley cropping between young trees ({{ref:soil-agri-134}}), then move to silvopasture, forest farming or an orchard. The other path is to trim the trees and keep alley cropping.
